title: Materials & Finishes
description: Material selection, plastics, metals, elastomers, finishes and coatings, compliance, contact materials, sustainability and outdoor durability.

items.text: Every part has its material chosen against written requirements for strength, stiffness and operating temperature range
items.hint: Trace each part's material back to the requirements list and load cases. A material picked by habit is the usual root cause of creep, cracking or softening found late in validation.

items.text: Every part specifies a specific grade (manufacturer and grade name), not a generic family like "ABS" or "aluminum"
items.hint: Check the drawing, BOM and CAD material field. Properties within one family vary widely, and a generic callout lets the supplier substitute whatever is cheapest.

items.text: Properties used for design are taken from the datasheet at the maximum operating temperature, not at 23 °C
items.hint: Look for modulus, yield and HDT versus temperature curves (e.g. on Campus or the supplier's data). Plastics can lose a large share of their stiffness well below their HDT.

items.text: Parts under sustained load have a material with documented creep or stress-relaxation behavior at the operating temperature
items.hint: Ask for creep modulus or isochronous stress-strain data from the supplier. Bosses, press fits and clips under constant load are the usual victims.

items.text: Chemical exposure (cleaners, disinfectants, oils, sunscreen, fuels, process fluids) is listed and every exposed material is rated for it
items.hint: Build the list from the use environment and cleaning instructions, then check the supplier's chemical resistance table for each pair. Mark any untested pair for an immersion or strain test.

items.text: Flammability requirement is identified and every part that needs it uses a material with the matching rating
items.hint: Check the product safety standard for which parts must be flame rated (enclosures, parts near ignition sources). Cross-check with the compliance engineer before tooling.

items.text: UV and light exposure is considered for every exposed part, including indoor exposure near windows or lighting
items.hint: Unstabilized polymers yellow, chalk and embrittle. Check the datasheet for UV stabilization or plan a weathering test.

items.text: Every specified material is available from stock or with a confirmed lead time in the production region
items.hint: Confirm with the molder, machine shop or distributor before release. Specialty grades and colors can carry long minimum order quantities and lead times.

items.text: Critical materials have an approved second source or an equivalent grade validated in advance
items.hint: Record the alternate grade in the BOM with its approval status. Switching grades after a shortage without retesting is a common cause of field failures.

items.text: Material cost per part is estimated and fits the cost target
items.hint: Use part volume or mass, scrap or runner allowance and current price per kg from the supplier. Flame-retardant, glass-filled and high-performance grades can change the part cost significantly.

items.text: Density and resulting part mass are entered in CAD and the total mass meets the product requirement
items.hint: Assign the real material to every part in CAD and check the mass report against the weight budget. Default CAD densities make mass rollups meaningless.

items.text: Material choices are recorded in a materials list with grade, supplier, color, finish and the reason for selection
items.hint: One table per product, kept with the design record. It speeds up compliance declarations and later substitutions.

items.text: Resin grade and color are called out together as one orderable specification (grade plus color code)
items.hint: A color code without a base grade, or a grade without a color, gets interpreted differently by each molder. Check the drawing title block and notes.

items.text: Effects of glass or mineral fill on anisotropy, warpage and weld line strength are accounted for in the design
items.hint: Filled grades have much lower strength across the flow direction and at weld lines. Review the gate location and mold flow fiber orientation results for loaded features.

items.text: Moisture absorption is accounted for in dimensions and properties for hygroscopic resins such as nylon
items.hint: Nylon grows and softens as it conditions to ambient humidity. Use conditioned properties from the datasheet and check fits in both dry-as-molded and conditioned states.

items.text: Parts that see chemicals while under molded-in or assembly stress are checked for environmental stress cracking
items.hint: Amorphous resins (PC, ABS, PC/ABS, acrylic) crack with cleaners, alcohols, oils and adhesives under strain. Use a strain jig or bent-strip test with the actual chemicals and the expected strain.

items.text: Regrind policy (allowed or not, maximum percentage) is stated on the drawing or in the supply agreement
items.hint: Regrind lowers impact and flame performance. Medical, flame-rated and highly loaded parts usually forbid it or cap it per the material supplier's guidance.

items.text: Colorant or masterbatch is confirmed not to degrade the required mechanical, flame or regulatory properties
items.hint: Some pigments and carriers reduce impact strength or void a UL listing. Use a precolored compound listed by the supplier, or get the colorant approved in writing.

items.text: UL 94 rating is verified at the actual minimum wall thickness and in the actual color of the part
items.hint: UL Yellow Cards list ratings per thickness and sometimes per color. A rating at 3 mm (118 mil) does not cover a 1.5 mm (59 mil) wall; check the thinnest section in CAD against the card.

items.text: Drying requirements of the resin are passed to the molder in the material specification
items.hint: Undried PC, PBT, PET and nylon hydrolyze during molding and become brittle with no visible defect. Reference the supplier's drying temperature and time.

items.text: Temperature limits use the right property (HDT, RTI or Vicat) for the kind of exposure
items.hint: HDT is a short-term deflection value, not a continuous use limit. For long-term elevated temperature use the relative thermal index or supplier aging data.

items.text: Material for living hinges, snap fits and press fits has enough elongation at yield for the design strain
items.hint: Check allowable strain from the datasheet or supplier guidance for the specific grade. Glass-filled and amorphous brittle grades often cannot survive repeated deflection.

items.text: Overmold and two-shot material pairs are confirmed compatible for adhesion by the material supplier
items.hint: TPE and LSR bond only to specific substrates. Get the supplier's compatibility chart or a peel test; otherwise design mechanical interlocks.

items.text: Additive parts specify process, material, build orientation and post-processing
items.hint: SLS, MJF, SLA and FDM parts are anisotropic and orientation sensitive. Put the orientation and post-cure or annealing on the drawing or build sheet.

items.text: Properties of additive materials used for design come from the printing vendor's data for the specific process and machine
items.hint: Generic datasheet values often overstate z-direction strength. Ask the service bureau for tested values or test coupons in the build orientation.

items.text: Transparent or light-pipe parts use an optical grade with defined transmission, haze and color stability
items.hint: Check the light transmission and yellowing index data in the datasheet. General-purpose grades of PC or acrylic can yellow and cloud over time.

items.text: Every metal part specifies alloy and temper or condition (e.g. 6061-T6, 304 annealed, 1/4 hard)
items.hint: Temper drives yield strength, formability and machinability. A missing temper on the drawing lets the supplier ship the softest condition.

items.text: Sheet-metal alloy and temper are confirmed formable to the bend radii in the design
items.hint: Hard tempers and some aluminum alloys crack on tight bends. Check minimum bend radius against the supplier's or material standard's table for that temper and thickness.

items.text: Every pair of dissimilar metals in contact is checked for galvanic corrosion in the expected environment
items.hint: Use a galvanic series chart for the electrolyte (moisture, salt). Isolate with coatings, washers or sealant, or keep the anode area large relative to the cathode.

items.text: Stainless steel grade is chosen for the actual environment (e.g. 316 for chloride or marine exposure instead of 303 or 304)
items.hint: Free-machining 303 and 400-series grades corrode much faster in chlorides. Check the corrosion requirement and cleaning chemicals.

items.text: Carbon and alloy steel parts have a defined corrosion protection
items.hint: Bare steel rusts in storage and transport. Check the drawing for plating, coating or oil, and that it suits the environment.

items.text: Magnetic properties are checked where parts are near magnets, sensors, compasses or MRI
items.hint: Austenitic stainless becomes partly magnetic after cold work or forming. Specify a low-permeability grade or annealing if it matters.

items.text: Die-cast alloy is chosen for the required ductility, corrosion resistance and finish
items.hint: Common die-cast aluminum alloys trade ductility for castability, and porosity can affect plating, anodizing and pressure tightness. Confirm with the caster.

items.text: Extrusion alloy and temper are confirmed with the extruder for the profile shape and finish
items.hint: Some alloys anodize poorly or show die lines. Ask the extruder which alloy suits the profile and the cosmetic requirement.

items.text: Weldable alloy and filler compatibility are confirmed for every welded joint
items.hint: Some high-strength aluminum alloys are poorly weldable and lose temper in the heat-affected zone. Use the welded properties in analysis.

items.text: Spring materials (spring steel, stainless spring temper, music wire) are specified with temper and fatigue suitability
items.hint: Check the spring supplier's guidance for the stress level and cycle count. Relaxation at elevated temperature is a common failure.

items.text: Elastomer compound is selected for compatibility with every fluid, lubricant and cleaner it contacts
items.hint: Check the compound's chemical compatibility chart (EPDM swells in oils, NBR degrades with ozone and UV). Lubricants used during assembly count too.

items.text: Elastomer compound is rated for the full operating and storage temperature range
items.hint: Check both ends: low-temperature stiffening (TR10 or brittleness point) and high-temperature aging in the datasheet.

items.text: Compression set at the operating temperature is acceptable for the sealing or preload function over the product life
items.hint: Use compression set data at the right temperature and duration from the supplier. A gasket that takes a permanent set loses its seal.

items.text: Durometer is specified with a tolerance consistent with supplier capability
items.hint: Rule of thumb: ±5 Shore A is a common supplier tolerance. Make sure the design still works at both ends of the range.

items.text: Elastomer compound is specified by compound name or supplier part number, not only by polymer and durometer
items.hint: "70A silicone" can be many different compounds. Specify the compound or a material standard callout and require change notification.

items.text: Keypad, grip and skin-contact elastomers are checked for tackiness, plasticizer migration and staining
items.hint: Some TPEs bleed oils that mark adjacent plastics or feel sticky after heat aging. Ask for heat-aging data or run a contact stain test.

items.text: Elastomer is confirmed suitable for its ozone and UV exposure
items.hint: Diene rubbers (NR, NBR, SBR) crack under ozone and UV. Silicone, EPDM and fluoroelastomers resist it better.

items.text: Anodize is specified with type, class or color, and thickness range
items.hint: Name the anodize type (e.g. sulfuric or hard coat), dye or clear, and thickness per the finisher's capability. An unspecified anodize gives inconsistent color and wear.

items.text: Dimensional growth of anodize, plating or coating is included in fits and tolerances
items.hint: Anodize grows partly outward per surface, and hard anodize much more. State whether dimensions apply before or after finishing on the drawing.

items.text: Masking areas are defined on the drawing for threads, bores, grounding points and mating faces that must stay bare
items.hint: Show masking with a hatch or callout in a drawing view. Unmasked threads and fits are a common rework item after first finishing.

items.text: Plating type and thickness are specified and suit the base metal and environment
items.hint: Specify the plating (zinc, nickel, tin) with thickness and any post-treatment per the plater's capability. Check hydrogen embrittlement relief for high-strength steels.

items.text: Powder coat or paint thickness is accounted for at fits, holes and threaded features
items.hint: Powder coat is thick and builds up at edges. Mask or oversize mating features and check stack-ups with the coating thickness per the coater's capability.

items.text: Paint or coating adhesion is specified with a test method and acceptance level
items.hint: Reference a cross-hatch or tape adhesion test and the required rating in the finish specification. Plastics often need a primer or surface treatment.

items.text: Stainless steel parts are passivated after machining or forming where corrosion resistance matters
items.hint: Free iron from tooling causes rust spots. Call out passivation and the method per the finisher's standard practice.

items.text: Grounding and bonding points have a conductive finish or a defined bare area
items.hint: Anodize, powder coat and paint are insulators. Use conductive chromate conversion, mask the contact area, or use a star washer, and verify resistance on the prototype.

items.text: Shielding coatings (conductive paint, plating on plastic) are specified with surface resistance and coverage area
items.hint: Coordinate with the EE on the resistance requirement and the contact points to the PCB ground.

items.text: PVD or other decorative hard coatings are specified with color, thickness and substrate preparation
items.hint: PVD replicates the substrate finish exactly, so polishing or blasting must be specified first. Confirm the wear and adhesion test with the supplier.

items.text: Mold texture is specified by texture supplier reference and checked against draft on every textured face
items.hint: Each texture needs a minimum draft angle per the texture supplier. Insufficient draft drags the texture and scuffs the part, and fixing it means retexturing the tool.

items.text: Pad printing, screen printing and laser marking are specified with the durability test they must pass
items.hint: Define abrasion, chemical rub (e.g. alcohol or cleaners) and adhesion tests in the artwork specification. Laser marking needs a laser-markable grade or additive.

items.text: Colors are specified against a named standard (Pantone, RAL, NCS) or a physical color master with tolerance
items.hint: Specify the measurement method, light source and allowed delta E. On-screen color is not a specification.

items.text: Approved color and finish samples (boundary samples) exist and are held by both Dovetail and the supplier
items.hint: Keep signed master and limit samples for color, gloss and texture. Without them cosmetic disputes at production start have no reference.

items.text: Gloss level is specified with a measurement angle and range for cosmetic surfaces
items.hint: Gloss mismatch between parts from different processes (molded, painted, metal) is very visible. Specify gloss units at a stated angle.

items.text: Finish process is compatible with the base material temperature limits and part geometry
items.hint: Powder curing, PVD and some plating processes run hot or need racking points. Confirm with the finisher that the part will not distort or soften.

items.text: Every material and finish is confirmed RoHS compliant with a supplier declaration on file
items.hint: Collect declarations for each part number, including coatings, inks and adhesives. Hexavalent chromate conversion coatings and leaded brass are common misses.

items.text: REACH SVHC content is checked against the current candidate list for every article
items.hint: The candidate list is updated regularly. Request SVHC declarations from suppliers and re-check before each release.

items.text: California Proposition 65 exposure is assessed where the product is sold in California
items.hint: Common triggers include certain plasticizers, flame retardants and lead in brass. Decide on warning labels or substitution early.

items.text: Conflict minerals (tin, tantalum, tungsten, gold) reporting needs are identified and supplier data is requested
items.hint: Use the customer's reporting template and collect supplier responses before production start.

items.text: Material declarations (full or IPC-1752 style) are requested from suppliers for every purchased and custom part
items.hint: Make declarations a deliverable in the supplier quote request. Chasing them after launch delays certification and customer audits.

items.text: Restricted substance requirements from the customer or target markets are listed and checked
items.hint: Customers often have their own restricted substance lists beyond RoHS and REACH (e.g. PFAS, halogens). Check them before material selection is final.

items.text: Flame-retardant additives in chosen grades are compatible with halogen-free or restricted substance requirements
items.hint: Brominated flame retardants may be restricted by customer specs. Check the grade's composition statement.

items.text: Materials used in safety-critical parts are on the certification body's accepted component list or have the required listing
items.hint: Enclosure plastics usually need a UL-recognized grade; a substitute grade often triggers retesting. Record the file number.

items.text: Every skin- or patient-contact material is identified with its contact type and duration
items.hint: Classify contact per ISO 10993-1 (surface, external communicating, implant) and duration. This drives the biocompatibility test plan.

items.text: Biocompatibility evidence per ISO 10993 exists or is planned for every contact material in its final processed form
items.hint: Supplier data on the raw resin is not enough by itself: colorants, processing, coatings and sterilization change the result. Use supplier master files and a biological evaluation plan.

items.text: Nickel release from metal parts in prolonged skin contact is assessed against the market requirement
items.hint: Stainless, plated and nickel-containing alloys can cause allergic reactions. Check the alloy and plating, and test release if needed.

items.text: Materials are compatible with the specified sterilization or disinfection method
items.hint: Gamma, EtO, autoclave and hydrogen peroxide each affect polymers differently (yellowing, embrittlement, crazing). Check supplier data and test after repeated cycles.

items.text: Material change control is agreed with suppliers for every contact material
items.hint: Require advance notification of any formula, site or process change in the supply agreement. Unannounced changes can invalidate biocompatibility.

items.text: Every wetted material is checked for compatibility with every medium, including cleaning and flushing fluids
items.hint: Build a wetted-materials matrix (tubing, seals, adhesives, housings, fittings) against media and temperature. Check swelling, extraction and stress cracking.

items.text: Required contact approvals (food, potable water, medical fluid path) are identified and every wetted material has them
items.hint: Identify which regulations apply in each market and get the supplier's compliance letter for the specific grade and color.

items.text: Leachables and extractables risk is assessed where fluid purity or taste matters
items.hint: Plasticizers, lubricants and mold release agents can contaminate the fluid. Ask suppliers for extractables data or plan a test.

items.text: Permeation of gases or vapors through tubing and housings is acceptable for the application
items.hint: Silicone and some TPEs are highly permeable. Check permeation data if the fluid can dry out, degas or absorb oxygen.

items.text: Wetted metal parts are chosen to avoid corrosion and ion release into the fluid
items.hint: Check the fluid chemistry (chlorides, pH) against the metal and its finish. Avoid platings that can flake into the fluid path.

items.text: Plastic parts carry a resin identification marking where space allows
items.hint: Mark per the applicable resin coding convention (e.g. >PC+ABS<) in a non-cosmetic area, and include it on the drawing.

items.text: The number of different materials is minimized and dissimilar materials are separable at end of life
items.hint: Review the materials list for near-duplicate grades that could be consolidated. Permanently bonded mixed materials are hard to recycle.

items.text: Recycled-content or bio-based material targets, if any, are met by grades with verified properties
items.hint: Recycled grades vary lot to lot. Get supplier data and certificates, and test critical properties.

items.text: Battery and electronics removal for end-of-life treatment is possible without destroying the enclosure
items.hint: Check against market requirements for removable batteries and WEEE treatment. Coordinate with the DFA review.

items.text: Exposed plastics are UV-stabilized grades and the color is confirmed for UV stability
items.hint: Check the datasheet for UV stabilization and ask the supplier for weathering data. Dark colors often hold up better; bright and light colors can fade or yellow.

items.text: Accelerated weathering test (xenon arc or UV fluorescent) is planned for exposed materials and finishes
items.hint: Define the method, duration and acceptance (color change, gloss retention, property retention). Coordinate with the validation plan.

items.text: Salt spray or cyclic corrosion resistance is specified for metal parts and finishes where required
items.hint: State the test method and duration per the product specification. Cyclic tests correlate better with real exposure than neutral salt spray alone.

items.text: Materials are rated for the outdoor temperature extremes including solar heating of dark surfaces
items.hint: Dark surfaces in sun get much hotter than ambient air. Use the analysis or field data to set the material temperature rating.

items.text: Fasteners and hardware exposed outdoors match the corrosion class of the parts they join
items.hint: A zinc-plated screw in a stainless or anodized assembly rusts first and stains the product. Check the fastener finish in the BOM.
